environment-responses-s1.title: Pill bugs in a moist-dry choice chamber
environment-responses-s1.html:
A student placed 10 pill bugs (small land crustaceans) in the center of each of ten round dishes and counted the animals on each half every 2 minutes. In five dishes, one half held moist filter paper and the other half dry paper. In five control dishes, both halves held dry paper. All dishes were at 22 °C under the same dim light. In a separate test, single animals were filmed for 5 minutes on all-dry paper or all-moist paper (10 animals each): on dry paper they spent a mean of 85% of the time walking, at 1.4 cm/s; on moist paper, 25% of the time, at 0.8 cm/s. Animals released exactly on the border between moist and dry paper walked into the dry half first as often as into the moist half.

energy-flow-ecosystems-s1.title: Energy budget of a lake food chain
energy-flow-ecosystems-s1.html:
Ecologists built a model of energy flow in a lake from field measurements, rounded for clarity. Phytoplankton (algae) are eaten by zooplankton, zooplankton by small fish, and small fish by fish-eating birds. Small fish are ectotherms; the birds are endotherms. For each level the table gives the energy taken into the body (absorbed from food, so not counting what leaves in feces; for phytoplankton, the energy captured by photosynthesis), the part released as heat by cellular respiration, and the part stored in new biomass (growth and offspring), which is the energy available to the next level.

biodiversity-s1.title: Species on rocky-shore plots after a predator is removed
biodiversity-s1.html:
On a rocky shore, a predatory sea star eats mussels, barnacles and snails. Researchers marked ten 4 m² plots. From five plots they removed every sea star each month for six years; five control plots were left alone. Each year they counted the species of attached animals and seaweeds in each plot. Sea stars made up less than 1% of the animals counted. Mussels covered about 20% of the rock in every plot at the start; after six years they covered 85% of the removal plots and 15-25% of the control plots. Points are means of five plots.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results in the table?
options: Most animals were already on the moist half at the first count, and that share stayed about the same through the full 10 minutes of counting.
The share on the moist half rose from 58% at 2 minutes to 82% at 10 minutes, while the control dishes stayed near half and half.
The share on the moist half rose over time, and the control dishes showed a similar steady rise in the count on half 1.
The animals moved onto the moist half in the first 2 minutes and then spread back out evenly between the two halves.

items.q: The null hypothesis is that the pill bugs have no preference, so equal numbers are expected on the two halves. Calculate the chi-square value for the moist-dry dishes at 10 minutes. Give your answer to one decimal place.
For two categories (df = 1), the critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84. Which conclusion about the 10-minute counts in the moist-dry dishes is best supported?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the chi-square value is larger than the critical value for one degree of freedom.
Reject the null hypothesis, which shows that pill bugs detect moisture with receptors located on their legs and antennae.
Reject the null hypothesis: the animals are not spread at random between the halves, which supports a response to moisture.
Accept the null hypothesis, because the control dishes show that the animals have no preference for either half of a dish.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the control dishes with dry paper on both halves?
options: To give a second moist-dry comparison, doubling the number of animals tested
To keep the number of animals equal in each dish so a statistical test can be used
To measure how many animals die on dry paper during the 10 minutes of counting
To check whether the dish, light or handling alone makes animals gather on one half

items.q: Which explanation fits all of the data, including the filmed animals?
options: On dry paper the animals keep walking and on moist paper they mostly stop, so they collect on the moist half without steering toward it.
The animals sense the direction of the moisture and walk straight toward it, which is why the count on the moist half keeps rising at each count.
The animals learn in the first minutes that the moist half is safer and then return to it from memory each time they leave.
Animals on the dry half lose water and stop moving, so they are not counted, and the dry-half number shrinks over the 10 minutes.

items.q: Based on rows 1 to 5, which statement correctly classifies species A and estimates its critical night length?
options: A short-day plant whose critical night length lies between 12 and 14 hours
A long-day plant whose critical day length lies between 12 and 14 hours
A short-day plant whose critical night length lies between 10 and 12 hours
A short-day plant that needs 16 hours of darkness before it forms flowers

items.q: Which pair of rows gives the strongest evidence that species A responds to the length of the night rather than the length of the day?
options: Rows 1 and 5, because the plants flower with 8 hours of light but not with 16 hours
Rows 5 and 6, because the day length is the same but breaking the night stops flowering
Rows 4 and 5, because species A flowers well under both of these long-night light and dark cycles
Rows 6 and 7, because far-red light given after the red flash restores flowering

items.q: Which explanation accounts for the results in rows 6 and 7 for both species?
options: Red light switches phytochrome to its active form, as daylight does; far-red at once switches it back, so the night acts unbroken.
The two flashes add 10 minutes of light, which lengthens the day enough to switch the response of each species.
Far-red light is a stronger signal than red light, so it makes the plants of both species flower whatever light they received just before it.
Red light damages the genes for flowering and far-red light repairs them, so the second flash undoes the harm from the first.

items.q: In a new treatment, species A gets 8 hours of light and 16 hours of dark, but the light period is interrupted in its middle by 2 hours of darkness. Predict the percentage of species A plants that will flower.
options: About 95% or more, because the longest unbroken dark period is still 16 hours
About 0%, because breaking the light period resets the plant's measure of day length
About 50%, because the plants now get two dark periods that add up to 18 hours
About 80%, as in row 3, because the plants receive 6 hours of light a day, less than in row 5

items.q: Why was the temperature held at 22 °C in every growth chamber?
options: Because temperature can also affect flowering, so fixing it isolates the light effect
Because a constant temperature makes the flowering percentage come out equal in each chamber
Because 22 °C is the temperature at which phytochrome changes to its active form
Because a steady temperature lets the plants sense day length from the daily cycle of warming

items.q: A short-day plant that flowers on a cycle of 9 hours of light and 15 hours of dark is given a 5-minute flash of red light in the middle of every night. Predict the effect on each quantity, compared with plants without the flash.

variables.name: Percentage of plants that form flowers
Amount of active phytochrome in the leaves just after each flash
Length of the light period at the start of each day
Longest stretch of unbroken darkness the plants receive

items.q: A hamster kept in constant darkness for three weeks started running on its wheel 18 minutes later each day than the day before. What is the period of its circadian rhythm, in hours? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Select the two behaviors that are innate.
options: A spider raised alone from hatching spins a normal web for its species the first time it builds one.
A rat presses a lever more and more often after each press is followed by a food pellet.
A dog salivates when it hears a bell that has rung just before each meal for weeks.
A male stickleback attacks a crude wooden model with a red underside placed in its territory.
A crow scolds one particular person who trapped it a year earlier but ignores other people.

items.q: Inside a dark hive, a honeybee forager's waggle run on the vertical comb points 60° to the left of straight up. Its waggle runs last longer than those of bees returning from a patch 500 m away. Where is the food?
options: 60° to the left of north, and farther than 500 m from the hive
60° to the left of the sun's direction, and closer than 500 m
60° to the left of the sun's direction, and farther than 500 m
60° to the right of the sun's direction, and farther than 500 m

items.q: Ants travel in a line between a sugar bait and their nest. A student wipes a 3 cm strip across the line with a cloth soaked in alcohol. Ants arriving at the strip stop and wander, then pick up the line again on the far side. Which best explains this?
options: The ants follow the sight of the ants ahead of them, and the alcohol strip hides those ants from view.
The ants follow a chemical trail laid by earlier ants, and wiping removed the signal over that strip.
The alcohol smell is a warning signal that makes the ants turn back toward the nest at the strip.
The ants navigate by the sun, and the wet strip changes how the sunlight reflects off the ground.

items.q: In a ground squirrel colony, adult females with a mother, sister or daughters living nearby gave an alarm call in 68% of predator approaches. Females with no close relatives nearby called in 21%. Callers are more likely than silent squirrels to be attacked. Which explanation best fits these data?
options: Calling helps the whole colony survive, so alleles for calling spread because they benefit the species as a whole, not just the caller.
Females with relatives nearby are older and have learned that calling scares predators away from the colony.
Females without relatives nearby see predators less often, and so they have fewer chances to give a call.
Calling saves relatives that share many of the caller's alleles, so alleles for calling near kin can spread despite the risk.

items.q: In winter, a hibernating ground squirrel's body temperature falls from 37 °C to about 4 °C, and its oxygen use falls to about 3% of its active level. Why does this let it survive for months without eating?
options: Cold denatures its enzymes, so cellular respiration stops until spring and no stored fuel is used up.
Cold air holds more oxygen, so each breath supplies enough oxygen for several days of cellular respiration.
Its cells switch from burning fat to burning glucose, which releases more energy per gram of fuel.
Its cells' reactions run slowly when cold, so it makes and uses far less ATP and burns its fat slowly.

items.q: Grass seedlings were lit from one side. Seedlings with an opaque cap over the top 2 mm of the shoot grew straight up. Seedlings with a clear cap over the tip, and seedlings with an opaque collar around the lower shoot but the tip uncovered, both bent toward the light. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Bending is caused by light striking the lower shoot directly, which makes the lit cells there elongate.
The opaque cap kept water from reaching the tip, which stopped the shoot from growing.
The tip detects the direction of the light, and a signal from the tip causes bending lower down.
A cap over the tip blocks the response, so the clear cap probably let in too little light.

items.q: Migratory warblers were kept indoors in cages for a year with constant food and temperature, under lights that changed day length as it changes outdoors. Each spring and autumn they hopped restlessly for weeks, facing the direction wild birds of their species fly. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The birds learned when to leave by watching wild birds of their species fly past outside.
A shortage of food is the main trigger for migration in this species of warbler.
The restlessness is unrelated to migration, because caged birds are unable to migrate.
Changes in day length, with food and temperature held steady, are enough for migratory behavior.

items.q: Put the events of phototropism in a shoot lit from one side in order.
options: Light from one side reaches the tip of the shoot.
Auxin moves toward the shaded side of the tip.
Auxin travels down the shaded side of the shoot.
Cells on the shaded side elongate more than cells on the lit side.
The shoot curves toward the light.

items.q: Goslings raised by a scientist from the moment they hatched followed him everywhere, and as adults they tried to court people instead of geese. This is an example of
options: habituation to a repeated stimulus that had no consequence
imprinting during a short sensitive period early in life
operant conditioning, because following was rewarded with food
a fixed action pattern set off by a red cue on the scientist

items.q: Males of two firefly species fly in the same meadow on summer nights. Species X males flash once every 5 seconds; species Y males flash twice in quick succession every 6 seconds. Females answer only the flash pattern of their own species. What role do these flashes most likely play?
options: They are chemical signals released with the light that attract the females of both species equally well.
They are learned from the mother, so the pattern differs from family to family.
They are visual courtship signals that let females find mates of their own species.
They warn predators that the fireflies taste bad, so they play no part in mating.

items.q: What percentage of the energy captured by the phytoplankton is released as heat by their own respiration? Give your answer to one decimal place.

Calculate the trophic efficiency from zooplankton to small fish: the energy stored in new biomass by the small fish as a percentage of the energy stored in new biomass by the zooplankton. Give your answer to one decimal place.
The phytoplankton store 10,200 kJ in new biomass, but the zooplankton take in only 4,100 kJ. Which best accounts for most of the other 6,100 kJ?
options: It is released as heat by the phytoplankton's respiration after the cells have grown.
It is destroyed by the zooplankton's digestive enzymes as they break down the algae cells.
Algae that die uneaten, and eaten algae lost in zooplankton feces, pass to decomposers.
It is stored as fat by the zooplankton, a store that the table does not include.

items.q: The small fish store 20% of the energy they take in (82 of 410 kJ), but the birds store 2% (0.8 of 40 kJ). Which best explains the difference?
options: The birds are endotherms, so they burn much of their food to make heat that keeps the body warm, and that energy leaves the food chain.
The birds are at a higher trophic level, and the second law of thermodynamics destroys more energy at each higher level of a chain.
The birds digest fish less fully than the fish digest zooplankton, so less of the fish they eat is ever absorbed into the body.
The birds store most of their energy as fat, and the table counts the energy in fat as heat released by cellular respiration.

items.q: Suppose the birds were replaced by a large predatory fish (an ectotherm) that also takes in 40 kJ per m² per year. Predict the energy it would store in new biomass.
options: About 0.8 kJ, the same as the birds, because both feed at the same trophic level
Much more than 0.8 kJ, because an ectotherm does not spend energy making body heat
Less than 0.8 kJ, because large fish need more energy to swim than birds need to fly
Zero, because a fourth trophic level has no energy left to store as new biomass in a lake

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: CO₂ rises steadily through each year and drops back to the same January level at the start of the next year.
CO₂ is highest in late summer and lowest in spring, and it shows no overall change from the first year to the second.
CO₂ rises and falls each year, peaking in May and lowest in September-October, while rising about 2 ppm overall.
CO₂ stays nearly constant for most of each year, except for a sharp drop during a single month in early autumn.

items.q: Which best explains the fall in CO₂ from May to September each year?
options: Warm summer air holds less CO₂, so CO₂ moves from the air into the ground.
In the northern summer, land plants take in CO₂ by photosynthesis faster than respiration releases it.
Decomposers are most active in summer warmth, and they take CO₂ out of the air as they break down detritus.
Animals hibernate in summer, so their respiration stops returning CO₂ to the air.

items.q: Using the May value of each year, calculate the yearly rate of increase in CO₂ concentration, in ppm per year. Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which process best explains why the concentration is higher in every month of year 2 than in the same month of year 1?
options: Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests add CO₂ faster than plants and oceans remove it.
The station's plants grow more slowly each year as the air at the station becomes colder.
The oceans give off more CO₂ each year as they slowly lose their dissolved carbon to the air above.
Volcanoes near the station release CO₂ in a steady stream that grows larger each year.

items.q: A second station at the same latitude in the Southern Hemisphere, where there is much less land, measures CO₂ over the same two years. Predict how its yearly cycle compares with the graph.
options: A larger yearly swing, peaking in May, because there is more ocean to release CO₂ there
The same swing at the same time of year, because the air of the two hemispheres is the same
No yearly swing and no rising trend, because the Southern Hemisphere has few people
A smaller yearly swing, with its low in the southern growing season, and the same rising trend

items.q: Giant tube worms near a deep-sea hydrothermal vent, 2,500 m down where no sunlight reaches, have no mouth or gut. Bacteria living inside them oxidize hydrogen sulfide from the vent water. What is the best explanation of how energy enters this community?
options: The worms absorb sugars that sink from sunlit surface waters and pass them to the bacteria.
The bacteria use energy from oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to build sugars from CO₂.
The heat of the vent water is captured by the worms and converted into chemical energy.
The bacteria break down dead worms and release the energy stored in their bodies.

items.q: A tropical forest has a gross primary productivity of 3,500 g of carbon per m² per year, and the trees use 60% of it in their own cellular respiration. What is the forest's net primary productivity, in g of carbon per m² per year? Give a whole number.

numeric.unit: g C per m² per year

items.q: Select the two processes that move carbon from organic molecules or rock-like stores into the atmosphere as CO₂.
options: Photosynthesis by algae in a pond
Cellular respiration by fungi breaking down fallen leaves
Burial of dead plants in a waterlogged swamp
Burning coal in a power plant
Formation of shells from carbonate dissolved in seawater

items.q: A farmer grows soybeans in a field one year and corn the next, adding no fertilizer. The corn grows better than corn grown after corn. Which explanation is best supported by the nitrogen cycle?
options: Soybean leaves take N₂ directly from the air and release it as nitrate through their roots.
Soybeans use less phosphorus than corn, so more phosphate is left for the next corn crop.
Bacteria in soybean root nodules fix N₂ into ammonium, and decaying soybean roots release it.
Soybeans act as denitrifiers, removing nitrate that would otherwise poison young corn plants.

items.q: A forest soil is treated with a chemical that blocks nitrification (the conversion of ammonium to nitrate) and does nothing else. Predict the effect on each quantity over the next few weeks.

variables.name: Nitrate washed from the soil into a nearby stream

items.q: In a pond, algae are eaten by snails and by mayfly larvae. Snails are eaten by crayfish. Mayfly larvae are eaten by dragonfly larvae and by sunfish. Dragonfly larvae are eaten by sunfish. Herons eat crayfish and sunfish. Which organism feeds at more than one trophic level?
options: Snails, because they eat algae and are eaten by crayfish
Crayfish, because they eat snails and are eaten by herons in the pond
Dragonfly larvae, because they eat mayfly larvae
Sunfish, because they eat mayfly larvae and dragonfly larvae

items.q: In a patch of open ocean at one moment, the phytoplankton weigh less (4 g per m²) than the zooplankton that eat them (21 g per m²). Over a year, which explanation allows this without breaking the rule that energy decreases at each trophic level?
options: The phytoplankton divide many times a year and are eaten almost as fast as they grow, so their yearly production far exceeds zooplankton production.
The zooplankton also carry out photosynthesis, so they make most of their own food and do not depend on the phytoplankton for it.
The rule holds on land but not in water, where the zooplankton capture more energy from the phytoplankton than the phytoplankton stored in a year.
The zooplankton store energy far more efficiently than the phytoplankton, so they pass up more energy than the phytoplankton captured.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the phosphorus cycle?
options: Phosphorus enters living things mainly when soil bacteria fix phosphorus gas taken from the air.
Phosphorus has no important gas form; it enters soil and water mainly by weathering of rock.
Phosphorus cycles mostly through the atmosphere, falling in rain as phosphate ions.
Phosphorus is released mainly by burning fossil fuels, which adds phosphate gas to the air.

items.q: A large forest upwind of a farming region is cut down and replaced by bare ground. Which change in the water cycle best explains why rainfall over the farms decreases?
options: Less water vapor enters the air by transpiration, so less condenses into rain downwind.
More water soaks into the bare soil, so the clouds that form above it hold more water.
Bare ground reflects less sunlight, so less water evaporates from the farms downwind of it.
Cutting trees releases water stored in their wood, which falls as rain right away.

items.q: A 20 g mouse and a 20 g lizard are kept at 20 °C with all the food they want. Over a week the mouse eats food containing 450 kJ and the lizard 40 kJ, and both keep the same body mass. Which claim do these data support?
options: The lizard digests its food far better, so it needs less of it to stay the same mass.
The mouse grows faster than the lizard, so it needs extra food to build new tissue.
The mouse uses far more energy, most of it for metabolic heat that keeps it warm.
Both animals use the same energy, but the mouse stores the extra food as fat each week.

items.q: Put these steps in order to trace a nitrogen atom from the air into a protein in a rabbit, through a plant that takes up nitrate.
options: Bacteria in the soil fix N₂ from the air into ammonium.
Nitrifying bacteria convert the ammonium into nitrate.
A clover root takes up the nitrate from soil water.
The clover builds the nitrogen into an amino acid.
A rabbit eats the clover, digests its proteins and uses the amino acids.

items.q: Decomposers return carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus from dead matter to the soil and air. Why can they not return energy to producers in the same way?
options: Decomposers keep the energy of dead matter stored inside their own cells for good.
Energy is destroyed when dead matter is broken down into CO₂ and water.
Producers already have more energy than they need, so they release it unused.
Energy leaves dead matter as heat, which producers cannot use to make sugar.

items.q: Which species shows a Type III survivorship curve, and what does its curve show?
options: Species P: most individuals survive to old age and then die within a short span of time
Species Q: the same fraction of the survivors dies in each of the age intervals of its life span
Species R: most individuals die very young, and the few that survive early on live a long time
Species R: the number of individuals that die stays the same in each age interval of life

items.q: How many of the 1,000 species Q newborns are still alive at 50% of the maximum life span? Give a whole number.
Species Q's curve is a straight line on this log scale, falling by 0.3 in every 10% of the life span. What does that mean about deaths in species Q?
options: About half of those alive at the start of each interval die during it, at every age.
The same number of birds, about 100, die in each 10% of the life span.
Death is most likely in old age, because the curve reaches 0 at 100% of the life span.
Deaths are spread evenly, so as many die in the first 10% as in the last 10%.

items.q: Which species most likely releases thousands of eggs per breeding and gives them no parental care, and why?
options: Species R, because so few young survive that only very large numbers of eggs leave survivors
Species Q, because it loses a steady fraction at each age and needs to replace them steadily
Species P, because most of its young survive and each one needs large amounts of food
Species P, because its adults die over a short span late in life and can then leave many eggs

items.q: A fish hatchery raises species R eggs and larvae in protected tanks and releases the young at 20% of the life span, after which they face the same conditions as wild fish. Predict how the survivorship curve of the hatchery fish differs from the wild curve.
options: It falls more steeply in the first 20%, because crowding in tanks kills more young fish.
It stays much higher over the first 20% and then declines slowly, like the wild curve does after 20%.
It is the same as the wild curve, because survivorship is fixed by the species' genes.
It becomes a Type I curve, staying high until 100% and then dropping sharply.

items.q: Use dN/dt = B − D to calculate the population growth rate during week 3, in beetles per week. Give a whole number.
Calculate the per capita growth rate during week 3, in per week. Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which statement about weeks 1 to 5 is supported by the data?
options: The per capita growth rate rises each week, so the population grows faster and faster.
The number added each week stays at about 100 beetles, as in linear growth.
The number added each week rises while the per capita rate stays at 0.50: exponential growth.
Both the number added and the per capita rate fall as the container fills with beetles.

items.q: Assume the population keeps growing with r_max = 0.50 per week. Use dN/dt = r_max N to predict the number of beetles at the start of week 6. Give a whole number.
Which condition is needed for this pattern of growth to continue for another 10 weeks?
options: The temperature slowly rises, so that the beetles' metabolism keeps speeding up.
Food and space stay plentiful, so the per capita birth and death rates do not change.
The beetles evolve a higher r_max each generation as the population becomes larger.
The number of births each week stays at about 130, the value measured in week 1.

items.q: A student counts dandelions in ten 1 m² quadrats placed at random on a 400 m² lawn and finds 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 4, 2, 5 and 6 plants. Estimate the number of dandelions on the whole lawn. Give a whole number.
Creosote bushes in a desert are spaced almost evenly, far apart. Seedlings that sprout near an adult bush usually die within a year. Which explanation best accounts for this dispersion?
options: Adult roots take up the scarce water from a wide area, so seedlings near them dry out and die.
Seeds fall straight down from the parent, so the young grow in tight groups around each adult.
Wind spreads the seeds at random, so the bushes end up scattered with no pattern.
Bushes grow best close together, where they shade each other's roots from the desert sun.

items.q: Select each situation that would most likely produce a clumped dispersion.
options: Mushrooms growing on a forest floor where a buried log is rotting
Penguins nesting just out of pecking reach of their neighbors
Dandelion seeds carried by wind onto an evenly mowed lawn
Desert shrubs whose roots draw water from a wide circle

items.q: Which is an example of semelparity?
options: An oak tree that produces acorns each autumn for 200 years
A human who has children at several different ages in adult life
A robin that raises two broods of chicks each summer for several years
A bamboo that grows for 60 years, flowers once, sets seed and dies

items.q: Species X reaches adulthood in 3 weeks, lays about 500 eggs and gives no care. Species Y reaches adulthood in 4 years and raises one young every 2 years. A flood kills 95% of each population. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Y will recover faster, because its well-cared-for young are more likely to survive the flood.
X will recover much faster, because its high r_max lets a few survivors multiply quickly.
Both will recover at the same speed, because both lost the same percentage of individuals.
Neither will recover, because a loss of 95% leaves too few individuals to reproduce.

items.q: Select the two traits typical of r-selected species.
options: Reproducing early in life
Producing many small offspring at a time
A long life span
Much care given to each offspring
Reaching maturity late

items.q: A population of 2,000 voles has 600 births and 400 deaths per year, with no migration. A new disease raises deaths to 700 per year but does not affect births. Predict the effect on each quantity.

variables.name: Number of voles one year later

items.q: A bacterial culture growing exponentially has r_max = 0.03 per minute and contains 4,000 cells. Use dN/dt = r_max N to calculate its growth rate, in cells per minute. Give a whole number.
Two populations of the same insect have the same r_max and are growing exponentially. Population A has 10,000 individuals and population B has 100. Which statement is correct?
options: B is growing faster, because a small population has more resources for each individual.
Both add the same number of insects per day, because they have the same r_max.
A adds 100 times as many insects per day, though both grow by the same fraction.
A grows more slowly per individual, because a large population has a lower r_max.

items.q: An island population of 500 lizards has 120 births, 90 deaths and 40 emigrants in one year, and no immigrants. How many lizards are there at the end of the year? Give a whole number.
Put these steps for estimating the number of plants in a field in order.
options: Measure the area of the field.
Place quadrats of known area at random positions in the field.
Count the plants inside each quadrat.
Calculate the mean number of plants per square meter.
Multiply the mean density by the area of the field.

items.q: A female sea turtle buries about 100 eggs and leaves; on average only one hatchling in a thousand reaches adulthood. An adult turtle may live for decades. Which survivorship pattern and explanation fit best?
options: Type I, because the adults live for decades once they reach full size
Type II, because turtles die at a steady rate from hatching to old age
Type I, because the mother protects her eggs by burying them deep in the sand
Type III, because most die as eggs and hatchlings but survivors live long

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: Both populations rise and fall in cycles of about 9 to 10 years, and the lynx peaks come 1 to 2 years after the hare peaks.
Both populations rise and fall in cycles of about 9 to 10 years, and the hare peaks come 1 to 2 years after the lynx peaks.
The hare population cycles over about 9 to 10 years, but the lynx population stays nearly constant throughout.
Both populations peak in the same years, so the two cycles move up and down together with no delay between them.

items.q: In year 4, what is the ratio of hares to lynx? Give your answer as hares per lynx, to the nearest whole number. (Remember that hares are plotted in hundreds.)
Which explanation best accounts for the lynx peaks coming after the hare peaks?
options: Lynx numbers rise only after hares become plentiful, because well-fed lynx raise more kits, and kits take time to be born and grow.
Lynx numbers rise first and frighten the hares into breeding faster, which then brings the hare peak one or two years later.
Lynx and hares both respond to the same weather, but lynx take longer to notice the change, so their numbers rise later.
Lynx eat the hares' food plants, so lynx numbers rise after the hares have finished eating the plants back.

items.q: A student claims the hare cycle is caused by lynx alone and that hare food plays no part. Which new study would best test this claim?
options: Count lynx for another 20 years and check that their peaks still follow the hare peaks.
Compare hare numbers in large fenced areas that keep lynx out, with and without extra food, to open areas.
Measure the body mass of hares caught by trappers in peak years and in low years.
Count the hares in one area each month instead of once a year to get more data points.

items.q: Starting in year 20, trappers remove nearly every lynx from the region and keep them out. Predict what happens to the hare population over the next several years.
options: Hares rise and stay at their year-4 peak of about 6,000 per 100 km² indefinitely.
Hares fall to near zero, because they depend on lynx to keep their food plants healthy.
Hares rise, then decline as they eat down their winter food, settling near what the plants support.
Hares stay at about 1,000 per 100 km², because removing lynx has no effect on them.

items.q: What is the best estimate of the carrying capacity of the standard-food cultures, and the evidence for it?
options: About 270 cells per mL, the density reached on day 6, when growth was fastest
About 1,000 cells per mL, the density the double-food cultures reached by day 14
About 500 cells per mL, where the density levels off from day 10 to day 16
About 250 cells per mL, half of the highest density reached by the cultures

items.q: For the standard-food cultures, r_max = 0.8 per day and K = 500 cells per mL. Use dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K to calculate the growth rate when N = 250 cells per mL, in cells per mL per day. Give a whole number.
During which interval were the standard-food cultures adding cells fastest, and why?
options: Day 0 to 2, because each cell then had the most food and the per capita rate was highest
Day 4 to 6, when the density passed about half of K and many cells still had enough food
Day 10 to 12, because the number of cells, and so the number dividing, was largest then
Day 14 to 16, because the cultures had adjusted to their medium after two weeks of growth

items.q: Which conclusion about the double-food cultures is best supported by the data?
options: Doubling the food doubled r_max, so the cultures grew twice as fast from day 0 and leveled off at the same density.
Doubling the food made no difference, because the error bars overlap at each point on the graph.
Doubling the food removed the carrying capacity, so these cultures kept growing exponentially to day 16.
Doubling the food raised the carrying capacity to about 1,000 cells per mL, while early growth was about the same.

items.q: For the comparison of the two food levels to be valid, which conditions should be the same in both sets of cultures?
options: The amount of food and the volume of medium in each culture
The starting density, the volume of medium and the temperature
The final density and the number of days the cultures were grown
The starting density and the number of cells counted on day 16

items.q: Select the two factors that are density-dependent.
options: A virus that spreads faster when caterpillars are packed closely on leaves
A hard frost that kills 30% of the caterpillars on a tree
Competition among songbirds for a limited number of nest holes
A forest fire that burns 60% of a lizard population's habitat
A hurricane that floods a marsh and drowns many of its voles

items.q: A deer herd of 800 lives in a reserve with a carrying capacity of 1,000. A summer drought kills 40% of the deer, and the plants recover fully the next spring. Predict each quantity the next spring, compared with before the drought.
A population of rabbits has r_max = 0.4 per year and a carrying capacity of 1,000. Use dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K to calculate its growth rate when N = 900, in rabbits per year. Give a whole number.

After a very wet year, the same rabbit population (r_max = 0.4 per year) has grown to 1,200, but the habitat can still support only 1,000. Use dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K to calculate the growth rate, in rabbits per year. Include the sign and give a whole number.

Radish seeds were sown at 4, 16 or 64 seeds per pot (same pot size, soil and light). After 5 weeks, the mean mass per plant was 12.0 g, 4.1 g and 1.2 g, and the total plant mass per pot was 48 g, 66 g and 77 g. Which explanation best fits these results?
options: Crowded plants share the same light, water and nutrients, so each gets less, and total mass levels off near what the pot can supply.
Crowded plants grow taller to reach the light and so put less mass into their roots, which were not weighed in this study.
Each pot can support a fixed number of plants, so most seeds in the crowded pots did not sprout.
Plants in crowded pots release chemicals that kill their neighbors, so the total mass per pot decreases as density rises.

items.q: Twenty goats are released on an island with dense, slow-growing shrubs and no predators. Twelve years later there are 3,000 goats, the shrubs are mostly gone, and the following year the herd falls to 300. Which explanation best accounts for the crash?
options: The herd grew past what the island could support and ate the shrubs faster than they regrew, lowering K.
The herd reached exactly its carrying capacity, and populations at K usually fall by about 90%.
A density-independent event is the likely cause, because density-dependent factors do not cause crashes.
The goats' r_max fell to zero after twelve years, because the herd became too old to breed.

items.q: What is the carrying capacity of an environment for a population?
options: The largest population the environment can support over time with its resources
The highest per capita growth rate the population reaches under ideal conditions
The population size at which the growth rate of the population is the highest
The total number of individuals of the different species living in the environment

items.q: Why does the growth of a population slow as it approaches its carrying capacity?
options: Individuals grow older, so the per capita birth rate falls with age regardless of food supply.
Individuals stop reproducing on purpose to avoid using up the resources around them.
The environment produces fewer resources as more individuals arrive and settle in it.
Each individual gets fewer resources, so per capita births fall and per capita deaths rise.

items.q: In a moose population, the per capita death rate from wolves was 4% per year at 0.5 moose per km², 9% at 1.0 per km² and 15% at 2.0 per km². In the same years, deep snow killed 6%, 5% and 6% of moose. Which claim do these data support?
options: Wolves are a density-independent factor, because they killed moose at each density studied.
Snow is a density-dependent factor, because more moose died of it in the densest years.
Wolves act as a density-dependent factor and snow as a density-independent one.
Both act as density-independent factors, because both killed less than 20% of moose.

items.q: A late spring frost kills about 40% of the aphids on a rose bush whether there are 100 aphids or 10,000. How is the frost classified, and why?
options: Density-dependent, because the frost killed many more aphids on the crowded bush
Density-independent, because it killed about the same fraction at both densities
Density-dependent, because aphids compete for warm spots during a frost
Density-independent, because a frost is unlikely to kill a large share of a population

items.q: A few deer reach an island with plenty of food. Put the events in order.
options: The herd grows almost exponentially.
Food available per deer starts to fall.
Per capita births fall and per capita deaths rise.
The herd's growth rate slows.
The herd levels off near the island's carrying capacity.

items.q: Owls hunt voles in a grassland. When voles are scarce, owls catch about 2% of them each month; when voles are abundant, owls switch from other prey and catch about 10% each month. How does this owl behavior affect the vole population?
options: It acts as a density-independent factor, adding the same small loss at each vole density.
It has no effect on vole numbers, because owls also eat other prey when voles are scarce.
It raises the vole carrying capacity, because owls remove the weakest voles from the grassland.
It removes a larger fraction when voles are dense, helping hold vole numbers down toward K.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares the two woodlands?
options: Woodland X has more species, and its beetles are spread more evenly among them.
Woodland Y has more species, but most of its beetles belong to a single species.
Both have the same richness, because the same total number of beetles was caught.
Woodland Y has more species and a more even spread, so it has the larger D.

items.q: What is the relative abundance of beetle species 1 in woodland Y, as a percentage? Give a whole number.
A student claims woodland Y has the more diverse beetle community because more species were found there. Which response is best supported by the data?
options: The claim is supported: richness is the measure of diversity, and Y has two more species than X.
The claim is supported, because a D of 0.43 shows Y has about half as many rare species as X.
The claim is impossible to judge, because the two woodlands contain different species of tree.
The claim is not supported: Y's D (0.43) is lower than X's (0.81), because one species dominates Y.

items.q: Over several years, species 1 in woodland Y falls from 120 to 20 beetles while the other species keep the same counts. Predict the change in woodland Y's Simpson's D.
options: D falls, because fewer beetles are caught in total.
D stays the same, because the number of species is unchanged.
D rises, because the beetles are spread more evenly among species.
D rises above 1, because the community becomes more diverse than X.

items.q: Why was it important to use the same number of traps for the same 7 days in both woodlands?
options: Sampling more finds more of the rare species, so unequal effort would bias the richness comparison.
Equal effort guarantees that each woodland gives exactly the same total number of beetles.
Beetles are active mainly in June, so a longer study would have caught few extra beetles.
The Simpson's index requires both samples to contain the same species of beetle.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: Alone, each species levels off at a steady density; together, A levels off a little lower and B rises at first, then declines toward zero.
Alone, each species levels off at a steady density; together, both species level off at about half their densities when alone.
Alone, each species keeps growing to day 20; together, B outgrows A after day 8 and A declines to a low but steady density.
Alone and together, A reaches about 400 cells per mL, while B reaches about 250 cells per mL in each of the tubes.

items.q: By what percentage is the density of species B on day 20 lower when grown with A than when grown alone? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the decline of species B when grown with A?
options: Species A eats species B, so B is killed faster than it can divide in the shared tubes.
Both eat the same limited bacteria, and A takes them more efficiently, so B cannot keep pace.
Species B needs a different food from A, and the tubes contained less of B's food.
Species B is harmed by the wastes of A alone, since the two species use different resources.

items.q: Species B is then grown with species C, which feeds on bacteria and yeast that settle at the bottom of the tube, while B feeds on bacteria floating higher up. Predict the result.
options: B declines to zero as it did with A, because any second species excludes it.
C declines to zero, because B now has the advantage it lacked against A.
Both persist, each at a density below its density alone, by partitioning the food.
Both reach exactly their densities when grown alone, because they do not interact.

items.q: What is the purpose of growing each species alone?
options: To double the number of tubes so the mean densities are more reliable
To show each species can grow in these conditions, so B's decline with A is due to A
To find out which species divides faster by watching just the first 2 days of growth
To keep the bacteria in the shared tubes from being eaten too quickly

items.q: Select each example of commensalism.
options: Cattle egrets catch insects that grazing cattle stir up; the cattle are not affected.
A tapeworm absorbs digested food in a dog's intestine, and the dog loses weight.
Bees collect nectar from flowers and carry pollen between them.
Two warbler species feed on insects at different heights in the same tree.
A lion kills and eats a zebra.

items.q: In a lake, bass eat minnows, minnows eat zooplankton, and zooplankton eat phytoplankton. All the bass are removed. Predict each quantity a year later.

variables.name: Phosphate carried into the lake by streams each year

items.q: Hoverflies cannot sting, but they have black and yellow stripes like stinging wasps. Birds that have been stung by a wasp tend to avoid hoverflies too. What is this an example of?
options: Müllerian mimicry, because both insects share a warning pattern
Camouflage, because the stripes help the hoverfly blend into flowers
Batesian mimicry, because a harmless species resembles a harmful one
Warning coloration, because the hoverfly is toxic and signals it

items.q: Two butterfly species that both taste bad to birds have evolved almost the same orange-and-black wing pattern. Why does sharing the pattern benefit both species?
options: Birds learn to avoid the pattern after fewer attacks, so fewer butterflies of each species are eaten while birds learn.
One species can stop making its bad-tasting chemicals, saving energy, because birds avoid the shared pattern.
The two species can now interbreed, which combines their toxins in hybrid offspring and makes both more toxic.
Birds confuse the two species, so they eat whichever species tastes less bad and leave the more toxic one alone.

items.q: On islands where finch species F lives alone, its mean beak depth is 10 mm; species G alone also averages about 10 mm. On an island where both live, F averages 12 mm and G 8 mm, and they eat seeds of different sizes. Which explanation best fits?
options: Each bird changes its beak during its lifetime by practicing on seeds of the size it eats most often.
Where the species meet, competition favored individuals that ate different seeds, so beaks diverged.
The shared island has mostly larger and smaller seeds, so both species changed beak size by the same amount.
The two species interbred on the shared island, and their hybrids had beaks of unusual sizes.

items.q: On a rocky shore, small barnacles of species A live only high on the rocks and large barnacles of species B live lower down. When B is scraped off the lower rocks, A settles there and survives well. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A's realized niche is larger than its fundamental niche.
A dies when kept under water for long periods.
B's fundamental niche includes the high rocks.
Competition with B restricts A's realized niche.

items.q: Which change would increase a community's species diversity while its species richness stays the same?
options: Individuals become more evenly spread among the species
One species becomes more common while the rest decline
A new species arrives and becomes very common
The total number of individuals doubles in each species

items.q: A deer eats leaves and twigs from a shrub, and the shrub regrows from its roots. A tick feeds on the deer's blood for several days. How are these two interactions classified?
options: Both are predation, because one species feeds on the other
Mutualism (+/+) and parasitism (+/−)
Herbivory (+/0) and commensalism (+/0)
Herbivory (+/−) and parasitism (+/−)

items.q: Ecologists added phosphate to three ponds and left three ponds unchanged. In the fertilized ponds, algae, zooplankton and small fish all increased. Which kind of control do these results show?
options: Top-down control, because the fish at the top increased the most
A trophic cascade, because each level changed in the opposite way
Bottom-up control, because more nutrients raised every level above
Competitive exclusion, because the algae outcompeted the fish for phosphate

items.q: Pike, a fish that eats minnows, are added to a lake. Put the events in order.
options: Pike eat many of the minnows.
The minnow population declines.
Zooplankton, released from minnows eating them, increase.
Zooplankton graze down the phytoplankton.
The lake water becomes clearer.

items.q: In a food web, a fox eats both rabbits and the weasels that also eat rabbits. A disease kills most of the weasels. Which prediction about rabbits, in the short term, is best supported?
options: Rabbits increase, because one of their predators is now much rarer.
Rabbits decrease, because foxes switch to eating rabbits and catch most of them.
Rabbits do not change, because foxes eat rabbits as well as weasels.
Rabbits decrease, because weasels used to protect rabbits from foxes.

items.q: What does a Simpson's diversity index close to 0 indicate about a community?
options: It has many species, each about equally common.
It has many species, each very rare.
It is made up almost entirely of one species.
Its species are being lost very rapidly.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: Species numbers fell in both kinds of plot, but more slowly in the control plots than in the removal plots.
The control plots stayed at 15-16 species, while removal plots fell steadily from 15 to 7 species over six years.
Removal plots lost most of their species in the first year and then held steady at about 14 species per plot after that.
Removal plots gained species as the mussels spread, rising above the control plots by year 6.

items.q: By what percentage did the number of species in the removal plots fall from year 0 to year 6? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the loss of species from the removal plots?
options: Without sea stars eating them, mussels spread over the rock and crowded out species that need space to attach.
Without sea stars, the snails and barnacles they ate became too numerous and starved, taking other species with them.
Removing the sea stars disturbed the rock surface each month, which killed many of the attached species.
Sea stars release nutrients in their wastes, and without them the seaweeds and animals had too little food.

items.q: Which claim about the sea star is best supported by the data?
options: It is a foundation species, because the community is built on its large numbers.
It is a keystone species, because a scarce species had a large effect on the community.
It is an ecosystem engineer, because it changes the physical structure of the rock it lives on.
It is a competitor of the mussels, because both use space on the rock.

items.q: In a second experiment, researchers instead removed one rare red seaweed from five plots for six years. Predict the result.
options: Species numbers fall to about 7, as in the sea star removal plots.
Species numbers rise, because the seaweed was a strong competitor for space.
Mussels spread over 85% of the rock, because they lose a food source.
Species numbers stay near the control level, apart from the lost seaweed.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship shown in the table?
options: Plots with more species produced less biomass but lost a larger share in the drought.
Plots with more species lost a smaller share in the drought but were slower to return to their earlier biomass.
Plots with more species produced more biomass, lost a smaller share in the drought and recovered more fully.
Plots with different numbers of species lost similar shares of their biomass in the drought.

items.q: Using the means, calculate the biomass left in the 16-species plots during the drought, in g per m². Give a whole number.
Using the error bars (± 2 SE), which conclusion about drought losses is best supported?
options: 8-species and 16-species plots differ clearly, because their means differ by 8 percentage points.
1-species and 16-species plots do not clearly differ, because both sets of error bars are large.
1-species and 16-species plots differ clearly, but 8-species and 16-species plots do not clearly differ.
No two kinds of plot clearly differ, because each mean has an error bar around it.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the smaller drought losses in plots with many species?
options: Plants in diverse plots shade the soil so well that drought does not reach their roots.
Diverse plots are more likely to include drought-tolerant species that keep growing and use resources the others leave.
Each species in a diverse plot grows more slowly, so each needs less water during a drought.
Diverse plots were watered more often by the researchers to keep the many species alive.

items.q: Why did the researchers choose the species for each plot at random from the pool of 18?
options: So that the effect measured is of species number, not of always including one especially hardy species
So that each plot ends up with exactly the same total number of plants after it is sown
So that the 1-species plots each contain the most drought-tolerant species in the pool
So that the plots with more species are planted in the wettest parts of the field

items.q: Beavers cut trees and build dams that flood a stream valley, creating a pond with marshy edges where frogs, ducks and water plants live. Which term best describes the beaver's role?
options: Foundation species, because beavers are the most abundant animals there
Producer, because beavers supply the energy that the pond relies on
Keystone predator, because beavers eat the strongest competitor present
Ecosystem engineer, because beavers physically reshape the environment

items.q: In a meadow, removing species X (2% of the plant and animal biomass) cut the number of species by half, while removing species Y (40% of the biomass) cut it by 10%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Y is a keystone species, because it makes up the most biomass in the meadow.
Neither is a keystone species, because removing either one lowered richness.
X is a keystone species, because its effect is far larger than its share of the biomass.
Both are keystone species, because removing either one of them changed the whole community.

items.q: On a savanna, elephants push over and eat young trees, which keeps the land open and grassy. Zebras and wildebeest graze the grass. All elephants are removed from a large fenced reserve. Predict each quantity ten years later.

variables.name: Number of grazing zebras and wildebeest

items.q: Select the two examples of ecosystem services.
options: Wild bees pollinating apple trees in nearby orchards
A factory producing fertilizer from nitrogen gas
A wetland filtering sediment and nutrients from river water
A farmer buying seeds of a new crop variety
A city building a concrete wall along a river

items.q: A banana variety grown worldwide for decades was propagated by cuttings, so every plant was a clone. A soil fungus spread through plantations and the variety was largely abandoned. Which explanation best accounts for the collapse?
options: Clones grow more slowly than plants from seed, so the fungus overtook them.
Bananas lack an immune system, so no banana plant can resist any fungus.
Cuttings carry the fungus from parent to offspring, so each clone started life infected.
Every plant had the same alleles, so none had a defense against the fungus.

items.q: A region contains oak woods, peat bogs, meadows and streams. This variety is an example of
options: genetic diversity
species evenness among habitats
relative abundance
ecosystem diversity

items.q: Reef P has 30 coral species, and one of them makes up most of the coral cover; its Simpson's D is 0.52. Reef Q has 22 coral species, all about equally common; its D is 0.95. Which claim is best supported?
options: Reef P is more diverse, because it has more species than reef Q.
The reefs are equally diverse, because both have over 20 coral species.
Reef Q is more diverse, because its species are much more evenly represented.
Reef Q is less stable, because a lower number of species means less diversity.

items.q: In one forest, three bird species eat the same kinds of insects. In another, one fig species is the only food source for many fruit-eating animals during the dry season. Which loss would most likely change its community more, and why?
options: Losing one insect-eating bird, because birds are higher on the food chain than trees
Losing the fig, because no other species fills its role and many animals rely on it
Losing one insect-eating bird, because insects would then multiply without limit
Losing either one changes its community equally, because each is one species

items.q: A summer of unusually warm water kills most of the reef-building corals on a reef. The heat itself does not harm the reef fish. Predict what happens to the reef fish over the next few years.
options: Fish species decline, because the coral structure they shelter and feed in breaks down.
Fish species increase, because the corals no longer compete with the fish for food.
Fish species stay the same, because the warm water did not harm the fish themselves.
Fish species decline at first and then recover fully within one year as the coral regrows.

items.q: Two lakes lose most of their fish in the same severe winter. Lake A, with 12 fish species, regains its earlier fish biomass in two years; lake B, with 3 species, takes seven years. Lake A shows greater
options: resilience, because it recovered from the disruption faster
species evenness, because its fish biomass returned to normal
carrying capacity, because it supports more species of fish
trophic efficiency, because its fish grew faster after winter

items.q: How does a keystone species differ from a foundation species?
options: A keystone species has an effect far greater than its numbers; a foundation species matters through its abundance and habitat building.
A keystone species is a producer at the base of the food web; a foundation species is a top predator that controls the others.
A keystone species makes up most of the biomass in its community; a foundation species is rare but influential in its effects.
A keystone species changes the physical environment; a foundation species affects others mainly by being eaten by them.

items.q: Which list gives the three levels of biodiversity?
options: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Producers, consumers, decomposers and detritus
Richness, evenness and Simpson's index
Population, community and ecosystem

items.q: Which statement best describes the data downstream of the outfall?
options: Algae and both oxygen readings fall below the outfall, reaching their lowest values at 3 km.
Algae rise to a peak at 3 km, and the gap between afternoon and dawn oxygen is widest there.
Algae rise to a peak at 3 km, and oxygen rises at dawn and at 3 p.m. by the same amount there.
Algae stay near upstream levels, while dawn oxygen falls steadily over the whole 10 km.

items.q: At 3 km downstream, how much higher is dissolved oxygen at 3 p.m. than at dawn, in mg/L? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the oxygen readings at 3 km?
options: Algae take up O₂ by day for photosynthesis and release it at night, so the stream is richest in O₂ just after dawn.
The fish farm releases O₂-poor water at night and O₂-rich water by day, so the readings at 3 km follow the farm's daily cycle.
Water warms during the day, and warm water holds more dissolved O₂, so readings are high in the afternoon and low at dawn.
By day the dense algae add O₂ by photosynthesis; at night algae and decomposers respire without it, so O₂ falls by dawn.

items.q: What is the purpose of the site 1 km upstream of the outfall?
options: It shows the stream's conditions without the farm's water, as a baseline for comparison.
It is where the nutrients released by the farm are most concentrated in the stream.
It measures how far upstream the algae from the bloom can swim each day.
It provides the site where dissolved oxygen is lowest, which sets the scale of the graph.

items.q: The farm installs a filter that removes most of the phosphorus from its outflow. Algae in this stream are limited by phosphorus. Predict the dawn oxygen at 3 km the next summer, compared with now.
options: Lower, because less phosphorus means less food for the decomposers in the stream
Higher, because fewer algae grow, so less O₂ is used by respiration and decay
The same, because the farm still releases nitrogen into the stream each day
The same, because dawn oxygen depends on temperature rather than on algae

items.q: How many times higher is the PCB concentration in large fish than in the small fish they eat? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the pattern in the table?
options: PCBs are made inside the bodies of predators from chemicals in their prey, so more PCBs form at each higher level.
Larger animals drink more lake water than smaller ones, so they take in more of the PCBs dissolved in the water each day.
PCBs stay in body fat instead of being excreted, and each consumer eats many times its own mass, so they concentrate.
PCBs break down slowly in small organisms but speed up as they move into larger ones, which makes them more concentrated.

items.q: How many times higher is the PCB concentration in gull eggs than in the lake water? Give your answer in millions, to one decimal place (for example, 3.2 for 3.2 million).
A student claims that because PCB levels in the lake water are tiny, the PCBs pose no risk to wildlife. Which response is best supported by the data?
options: The claim is supported, because 0.000004 ppm is far too low to harm any organism.
The claim is not supported, because gull eggs carry 90 ppm, over 20 million times the water level.
The claim is supported, because PCB levels in phytoplankton are below those in fish.
The claim is not supported, because the water level is higher than in the phytoplankton.

items.q: PCB releases into the lake stop, and PCB levels in the water fall within a few years. Predict which samples will take longest to return to low PCB levels.
options: Phytoplankton, because they are closest to the water and absorb PCBs directly
Zooplankton, because they reproduce faster than the other consumers in the lake
Lake trout and gulls, because they are long-lived and keep stored PCBs in their fat
Lake water, because PCBs dissolve more easily in water than in living tissue

items.q: Zebra mussels from Europe reached North America's Great Lakes in ships' ballast water and spread rapidly, while native mussels declined. Which explanation best accounts for their success?
options: Native mussels were already extinct before zebra mussels arrived, leaving the lakes empty of competitors.
They are larger and stronger than the native mussels, so they win most contests for space on the rocky lake bottom.
Ballast water made them more fertile, and the effect lasted for several generations after they arrived.
They left behind the predators and parasites that limit them in Europe, and natives had few ways to resist them.

items.q: The CO₂ concentration of the air above an ocean region keeps rising. Predict the effect on each quantity in the surface seawater over the following decades.

variables.name: Carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) available to shell-building animals
Rate at which oysters build their shells
Number of chromosomes in each oyster's cells

items.q: In a forest, oak caterpillars now hatch about two weeks earlier than 40 years ago because springs are warmer. A songbird that feeds caterpillars to its chicks still lays its eggs at about the same date, timed by day length. Which effect on the songbird is most likely?
options: Chicks get more food, because warmer springs produce more caterpillars for longer.
Chicks hatch earlier too, because warm weather speeds up the incubation of the eggs.
Chicks hatch after the caterpillar peak, so food is short and fewer chicks survive.
Chicks are unaffected, because adult birds can switch to eating seeds in warm years.

items.q: A 100 km² forest is cut into twenty separate 1 km² patches with farmland between them, keeping 20 km² of forest. Ten years later, the patches together hold fewer bird species than a single 20 km² block nearby. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: The farmland adds new bird species, which take over the patches and push most of the forest birds out of them.
Birds in small patches reproduce faster, use up their food sooner and then starve within a few years.
The patches receive less sunlight than a large block, so their trees produce less food for birds.
Small patches hold small populations that are easily lost, and many forest birds avoid the hot, windy edges.

items.q: Cod off Newfoundland were fished heavily until the population collapsed and fishing was stopped. Decades later, the population was still far below its earlier size. Which explanation is best supported by population ecology?
options: Cod mature slowly, and the food web changed while they were scarce, so recovery has been slow.
Once a population is heavily fished, its r_max falls to zero and the survivors stop reproducing.
The ban on fishing raised the cod carrying capacity, so the population is now too crowded to grow.
Cod are r-selected, so their numbers stay low for decades after a large fall in population.

items.q: During an El Niño event, warm surface water off the coast of Peru stops the usual upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep. Predict the effect on the coastal food web.
options: Phytoplankton bloom in the warm water, so anchovies and seabirds increase that year.
Phytoplankton decline, so anchovies and the seabirds and sea lions that eat them decline.
The sea lions are the main species affected, because warm water raises their body temperature.
Nothing changes, because the warm water does not reach the bottom of the ocean.

items.q: Select the two human activities that add CO₂ to the atmosphere.
options: Burning natural gas to generate electricity
Clearing and burning a tropical forest for pasture
Planting trees on abandoned farmland
Generating electricity with wind turbines
Restoring a peat bog by blocking its drains

items.q: A power plant takes in river water to cool its machinery and returns it 8 °C warmer. Downstream, trout become scarce. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen, which is toxic to trout at high concentrations in the river.
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and a warmer trout needs more oxygen.
Warm water flows faster than cold water, so trout are unable to swim against the current near the plant.
Warm water kills the algae, so the river has no producers and trout have nothing to eat.

items.q: Put the steps of eutrophication in a coastal sea in order.
options: Heavy rain washes fertilizer from farm fields into rivers.
Nitrate and phosphate reach the sea and algae multiply.
Masses of algae die and sink to deeper water.
Decomposers break down the dead algae, using dissolved oxygen.
Fish leave the area and bottom animals suffocate.

items.q: In the 1960s a large lake had frequent algal blooms and low-oxygen bottom water. After phosphate was limited in detergents and sewage treatment improved, phosphorus entering the lake fell by about 60% within ten years, and blooms and low-oxygen areas shrank. Which claim do these data best support?
options: Low oxygen in the bottom water caused the algal blooms, rather than being a result of the blooms.
Detergents killed the algae directly, so removing them had no effect on the blooms.
Phosphorus was limiting algal growth in the lake, and cutting it reduced eutrophication.
Nitrogen, not phosphorus, limited the algae, because blooms continued at a lower level.

items.q: Which kind of pollutant is most likely to biomagnify?
options: A water-soluble chemical that the kidneys excrete within a day of exposure
A fat-soluble chemical that is broken down very slowly in the body
A gas that leaves the water quickly and enters the air above a lake
A chemical that decomposers break down within a week in soil

items.q: Which of the following is a natural disturbance rather than a human impact?
options: A volcanic eruption that buries a forest in ash
Runoff of fertilizer into a lake from farm fields
Release of cane toads into a sugar-cane region
Clearing a wetland to build a shopping center
